payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Who Was in the Room: Why Hollowmere Should Teach Chart Literacy

¶1 Last March, at a hearing of the Hollowmere County Council, a single chart nearly closed three branch libraries. The chart showed a line plunging from the upper left corner to the lower right, labeled Library Visits, 2019 to 2024, and several council members cited it in their remarks before the vote. The slide omitted one detail: its vertical axis began not at zero but at 410,000, so that a decline of about six percent looked, from the back of the room, like a collapse. The branches stayed open only because a retired surveyor in the audience asked to see the numbers behind the picture. This brief argues that the Hollowmere Unified School District should not leave such questions to the luck of who happens to be in the room.

¶2 We use the term chart literacy to mean the ability to read a data visualization as an argument rather than as a fact: to ask who drew it, what was left out, and what the chosen scale, color, and shape are doing to the viewer's judgment. It is not statistics, though it borrows from statistics, and it is not graphic design, though it borrows from that too. It is closer to the habit a careful reader brings to an editorial, the reflex of asking what the writer wants you to feel before you decide whether to feel it. Our recommendation is that this habit be taught deliberately, in a required unit for ninth and tenth graders, rather than assumed to arrive on its own.

¶3 The need is not speculative. In the spring of 2025, our office administered a short diagnostic to 1,140 students across four district high schools. Each student saw two bar charts describing the same fictional survey; one used a truncated axis and the other did not. Sixty-eight percent of students described the two charts as showing very different results, and fewer than one in five noticed the axis at all. When the same students were given five minutes of instruction on axis conventions and shown a third pair, the share who caught the truncation rose to just over half. Five minutes moved the needle; a semester, we believe, could move it much further.

¶4 Some members of the curriculum committee have reasonably asked whether this material belongs in an already crowded year, and whether it is really distinct from what mathematics teachers already cover. The concern about time is fair, and we do not propose adding a course; we propose a four-week unit that can live inside the existing civics or English sequence, where students are already learning to weigh sources. The concern about overlap is, we think, mistaken. Mathematics classes teach students to build charts correctly; almost no class teaches them what to do when someone else has built a chart incorrectly, or built it correctly and chosen the frame with care. The difference is the difference between learning to cook and learning to tell when a restaurant is hiding something under the sauce.

¶5 Consider how much of a citizen's year now arrives as a picture. Rent trends arrive as a line; crime arrives as a heat map; a candidate's record arrives as a pair of bars, one towering and one squat. These pictures are efficient, and we do not want students to distrust them wholesale, since a well-made chart can tell the truth faster than a paragraph can. But efficiency cuts both ways. A picture that persuades in two seconds also deceives in two seconds, and it leaves no sentence a reader can point to and call false.

¶6 The remainder of this brief sets out the proposed unit: four weeks of lessons, a cost of roughly 38 dollars per student, and the results of a pilot at Fenwick Ridge High School. We ask the board to read those sections with the surveyor in mind. He was not an expert; he simply knew which question to ask, and he was there. The district can make sure that, next time, a few hundred more people are.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
The Widow's Ledger

¶1 On a Tuesday evening in March, the Halverton City Council spent forty minutes debating whether a schoolteacher named Priya Castellanos could keep two hives on the roof of her garage. I sat in the back row with a folder of photocopies from the municipal archive, where I have worked for eleven years, and listened to a councilman warn that bees "do not belong in a modern city." He said it as if the matter were settled, as if modern and bee were words that had never shared a sentence. They have shared a great many, and most of them were written in Halverton.

¶2 The first beekeeper in our records was not a farmer but a tanner's widow, Agnes Durrow, who in 1891 set four straw skeps against the brick wall behind her rowhouse on Cordage Street. Her ledger survives, and it is a modest, stubborn document: so many pounds of honey sold to the druggist, so many to the bakery, a jar given to the priest, a sting noted and then forgotten. By 1905 the city directory listed nineteen households that kept bees, and the honey they produced was dark and faintly mineral, flavored by the linden trees the city had planted along the trolley lines. The bees, in other words, did not merely tolerate the city; they ate it, and gave something back.

¶3 Then came 1923. A boy on Fulling Lane was stung several times after poking a hive with a broom handle, and the Halverton Evening Courier ran the story under a headline that called the bees "a swarm of menace." Within a month the council passed an ordinance forbidding hives within the city limits, and within a year the nineteen households had become none. Nothing had changed about the bees. What had changed was the story the city told about itself: it was becoming a place of paved streets and electric signs, and a straw skep behind a rowhouse looked, suddenly, like a thing left over from a slower century. The ban was less a response to danger than a tidying away of the past.

¶4 I do not want to pretend the worries were all invented. Bees sting, and a hive placed on a fire escape above a crowded sidewalk is a poor neighbor; the boy on Fulling Lane spent two days in bed, and his mother's anger was neither foolish nor small. But a city that outlawed every creature capable of causing two days in bed would have to begin with its horses, its trolleys, and its own citizens. The question was never whether bees could do harm. The question was whether the harm was large enough to justify erasing a practice that fed bakeries, pollinated gardens, and gave a tanner's widow a trade of her own.

¶5 The practice did not stay erased. In 1974 a retired machinist named Oscar Lindqvist quietly installed a hive on the roof of a shuttered hat factory, and the inspectors who discovered it three summers later could not bring themselves to write him up. The ordinance was repealed in 1981, and the hives came back the way weeds come back to a vacant lot, first in one place, then in a dozen, then everywhere the sun reached. Today the archive holds photographs of hives on the library roof, in the courtyard of the firehouse, and behind the same rowhouse on Cordage Street where Agnes Durrow kept hers.

¶6 So when the councilman says bees do not belong in a modern city, I want to hand him the ledger. Bees have belonged to Halverton for longer than its sewers, its streetlights, or its council chamber. What they ask of us is small: a roof, a water dish, a measure of patience with the occasional sting. What they offer in return is a reminder that a city is not only pavement and ordinance but a living thing, and that the people who tend small, stubborn, useful work in its corners are not relics of a slower century. They are the ones who keep it alive.

provenance.note: Entirely fictional city, people, newspaper, dates and figures invented for this exercise.

blueprint.speaker: Theodora Vasic, a municipal archivist in the fictional city of Halverton who has spent eleven years with the city's records and writes with wry, grounded authority
blueprint.audience: Educated general readers of a city-interest quarterly, including local residents and council members who may assume beekeeping is a rural or outdated practice
blueprint.exigence: A council hearing debating whether a schoolteacher may keep two hives on her garage roof, during which a councilman declared that bees 'do not belong in a modern city'
blueprint.purpose: To use the archival history of beekeeping in Halverton to show that bees have always been part of the city's modern life, that the earlier ban was driven by self-image rather than danger, and that the current proposal rests on a mistaken assumption
blueprint.context: Historical-narrative essay published in a fictional city quarterly; traces beekeeping from 1891 through a 1923 ban, a 1981 repeal, and the present day
blueprint.claim: Bees have belonged to Halverton for longer than its modern infrastructure; the city's periodic impulse to ban them reflects anxiety about appearing modern, not a proportionate response to harm
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Paragraph 1 establishes the hearing and the councilman's assumption; paragraph 2 narrates the earliest records to prove bees and the city coexisted productively; paragraph 3 explains the 1923 ban as a story the city told about itself rather than a response to danger; paragraph 4 concedes that stings and poorly placed hives are real problems, then reframes the issue as one of proportion; paragraph 5 narrates the practice's survival and return after repeal, undermining the 'relic' idea; paragraph 6 returns to the councilman and states the thesis directly, ending on what bees ask and offer
evidence_types: historical anecdotes (Agnes Durrow, the 1923 boy, Oscar Lindqvist)

devices.function: Mocks the councilman's certainty by treating 'modern' and 'bee' as words supposedly never joined, which the next sentence immediately refutes
Agnes Durrow's skeps and ledger make the earliest beekeeping concrete and humanize it as a widow's trade
Bees 'ate' the city and 'gave something back,' framing the relationship as reciprocal rather than tolerated
Abrupt short sentences mark the turn to the ban, isolate the key point that the bees had not changed, and deliver the closing line with force
The stung boy and the newspaper headline supply the trigger for the ban and show how small an incident started it
Incident leads to headline leads to ordinance leads to disappearance of all hives, showing the speed and disproportion of the reaction
Colons open onto the explanation of the city's self-image and onto the short list of what bees require
The ban as 'a tidying away of the past' recasts regulation as housekeeping driven by image
Admits stings and bad placement are real problems, then rebuts by showing that the same standard would outlaw horses, trolleys and citizens
Lists of horses, trolleys, citizens; of bakeries, gardens, a trade; of hive locations make the argument concrete and cumulative
'The question was never... The question was whether...' reframes the issue from possibility of harm to proportion of harm
Opposes the wrong question to the right one
Oscar Lindqvist's illicit hive and the inspectors' reluctance show the practice surviving and public sympathy shifting
Hives returning 'the way weeds come back to a vacant lot' suggests irrepressible, natural resurgence
'What they ask of us... What they offer in return...' balances small demand against larger gift, framing the exchange as favorable
Bees set beside sewers, streetlights and the council chamber to show they predate the very markers of modernity

tone_shifts.to: direct, pointed resolution addressed to the councilman's claim

blueprint.counterargument: Bees sting and hives placed carelessly above crowded sidewalks are genuine nuisances; the 1923 boy's injury and his mother's anger were legitimate. The writer concedes this fully, then argues the harm is too small to justify erasing a productive practice, since the same standard would ban horses, trolleys and citizens.

items.stem: In the final paragraph, the writer begins two consecutive sentences with "What they ask of us" and "What they offer in return." This parallel structure primarily serves to

The correct answer is "set the modest requirements of bees against the larger return they provide, framing the exchange as plainly favorable to the city". The matched openings invite direct comparison; the first sentence's colon lists only a roof, a water dish and patience, while the second expands into a reminder that the city is a living thing, making the trade appear obviously worthwhile.

issues.issue: Internal chronology slip: ¶5 says the hive was installed in 1974 and discovered 'three summers later' (1977), yet the hives are described as returning only after the 1981 repeal; also Lindqvist's hive predates repeal, which is fine, but the 'came back' narrative is slightly muddled.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Leave Tuesday Empty

[1] Every Tuesday at Marlow Ridge High, the twenty-five minutes after lunch belong to nobody. [2] There is no lesson and no club meeting, and phones stay in the gray caddies by the door. [3] Next month the student council will vote on whether to fill this "quiet block" with scheduled enrichment sessions. [4] Boredom is an interesting topic that people have many different opinions about.

[5] Last spring I spent one quiet block staring at a water stain on the ceiling of Room 114. [6] By the end of it, I had sketched the plot of a short story that later won second place in the district writing contest. [7] My friend Dara Pell says she drafted half of her college essay during quiet blocks in October.

[8] Supporters of the change argue that unstructured time is wasted time. [9] They point out that some students just sleep or doodle. [10] But sleeping and doodling are not necessarily failures. [11] Honestly, the council needs to chill out and not ruin the one good thing about Tuesdays.

[12] The quiet block is something that is a period of time when students are able to think about things in a way that they choose themselves without being told what to think about. [13] So, that's my opinion on boredom.

My friend Dara Pell says she drafted half of her college essay during quiet blocks in October.
Supporters of the change argue that unstructured time is wasted time.
They point out that some students just sleep or doodle.

payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage
Forty Years on 89.7

[1] Radio is a thing that many people have listened to over the years. [2] This Saturday, Riverbend Community Radio turns forty, and its volunteers will spend the weekend asking listeners for enough money to replace a transmitter older than most of its DJs. [3] I think the town should give generously, because the little station on Kettle Street does something no streaming app can do.

[4] Streaming services know what I like, but they do not know where I live. [5] When the Oxbow River flooded in March, it was 89.7 FM that told us which roads were closed and which church basement had dry cots. [6] Volunteer Hal Pruitt stayed on the air for nineteen hours, reading messages from neighbors looking for lost dogs and elderly parents. [7] Every single person in Harrow Bend was listening that night. [8] No algorithm will ever do anything useful for a small town.

[9] The station is also a kind of town square. [10] On Tuesday nights, high school students host a show about their marching band's season, and on Sunday mornings retired farmers argue about rainfall totals. [11] The station's budget is pathetic, and frankly the fact that it survives at all is kind of a joke. [12] Yet it does survive, because ordinary people keep it going.

[13] The pledge drive runs from 6 a.m. Saturday until midnight Sunday, a donation of 25 dollars keeps the station on the air for about an hour. [14] So, that's my opinion on radio.

el_passage.title: Forty Years on 89.7
paragraphs: Radio is a thing that many people have listened to over the years.
This Saturday, Riverbend Community Radio turns forty, and its volunteers will spend the weekend asking listeners for enough money to replace a transmitter older than most of its DJs.
I think the town should give generously, because the little station on Kettle Street does something no streaming app can do.
Streaming services know what I like, but they do not know where I live.
When the Oxbow River flooded in March, it was 89.7 FM that told us which roads were closed and which church basement had dry cots.
Volunteer Hal Pruitt stayed on the air for nineteen hours, reading messages from neighbors looking for lost dogs and elderly parents.
Every single person in Harrow Bend was listening that night.
No algorithm will ever do anything useful for a small town.
The station is also a kind of town square.
On Tuesday nights, high school students host a show about their marching band's season, and on Sunday mornings retired farmers argue about rainfall totals.
The station's budget is pathetic, and frankly the fact that it survives at all is kind of a joke.
Yet it does survive, because ordinary people keep it going.
The pledge drive runs from 6 a.m. Saturday until midnight Sunday, a donation of 25 dollars keeps the station on the air for about an hour.
So, that's my opinion on radio.

issues.issue: Sentence order in the planned flaws lists id 12 before id 11, but the passage places them in sentence order (11 then 12). This is harmless. Both planned flaws are present and match the blueprint: S11 is flippant, S12 has no example.
The stray header line 'ALTON original passage' is a production artifact and should be removed before delivery. It is not part of the column.

Sentence 13 states a $25 donation keeps the station on air for about an hour. This is plausible but unsupported. It is acceptable as a fictional local detail, and the passage is clear that it is a local, invented station.

Sentence 14 ('So, that's my opinion on radio.') is a deliberately weak conclusion, as planned. The passage is otherwise coherent: it has a clear purpose, a local audience, a consistent claim, and a plausible columnist voice with concrete details (Kettle Street, Hal Pruitt, the Oxbow flood). It reads as human and not stock AI prose.

Sentence 7 ('Every single person in Harrow Bend was listening') and sentence 8 ('No algorithm will ever do anything useful') are deliberate overstatements per the blueprint. They are clearly fixable by modifiers or concession and do not make the passage unusable as a revision exercise.
